Reference: Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw (2001)

Model Setting

The paper studies the regression-discontinuity (RD) design, a quasi-experimental data design whose defining feature is that the probability of receiving treatment changes discontinuously as a function of one or more underlying variables. Such designs arise whenever programme rules or geographic boundaries create a jump in the treatment assignment mechanism. The examples cited are Thistlethwaite and Campbell (1960), who use a test-score threshold for scholarship awards; Van der Klaauw (1997), who uses aid rules that are discontinuous in grade point average and SAT score; Angrist and Lavy (1999), who use a rule that adds a classroom when class size exceeds a threshold; and Black (1999), who compares house prices near school attendance boundaries. Two questions were open: what the source of identification is, and how to estimate the treatment effect under minimal parametric restrictions.

The paper makes three points. First, the identifying conditions used in earlier applications are stronger than necessary: the treatment effect at the discontinuity point is nonparametrically identified by a weak functional form restriction, namely continuity of a conditional mean at the threshold. The restriction is unusual in that continuity is imposed in order to exploit a known discontinuity. With heterogeneous effects the same ratio of jumps identifies the average effect at the threshold under local conditional independence, or a local average treatment effect under local monotonicity in the sense of Imbens and Angrist (1994). Second, the treatment effect is a ratio of differences of one-sided limits, and the paper proposes to estimate the limits by local linear regression, which avoids the poor boundary behaviour of standard kernel estimators; an appendix gives the asymptotic distribution of the resulting estimator. Third, with one-sided uniform kernels the RD estimator is numerically equal to a Wald estimator, so the RD design can justify a Wald estimator even when the usual instrumental variable assumption fails. The paper is a short theoretical note and contains no empirical application of its own; the proof of the distribution theorem is delegated to a working paper, Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw (1999).

Outcome Model and the Two Designs

The goal is to determine the effect of a binary treatment xix_ixi​ on an outcome yiy_iyi​. Let y1iy_{1i}y1i​ be the outcome with treatment and y0iy_{0i}y0i​ the outcome without treatment, and let xi=1x_i=1xi​=1 if treatment is received and xi=0x_i=0xi​=0 otherwise. No individual is observed in both states. The observed outcome is:

yi=αi+xi⋅βi,αi≡y0i,βi≡y1i−y0i(1)y_i=\alpha_i+x_i\cdot\beta_i,\qquad\alpha_i\equiv y_{0i},\qquad\beta_i\equiv y_{1i}-y_{0i} \tag{1}yi​=αi​+xi​⋅βi​,αi​≡y0i​,βi​≡y1i​−y0i​(1)

In the sharp design, treatment is a known deterministic function of an observable variable ziz_izi​, written xi=f(zi)x_i=f(z_i)xi​=f(zi​), where ziz_izi​ takes a continuum of values and the point z0z_0z0​ at which f(z)f(z)f(z) is discontinuous is known. In the fuzzy design, xix_ixi​ is a random variable given ziz_izi​, because variables unobserved by the econometrician also determine assignment, but the conditional probability of treatment:

f(z)≡E[xi∣zi=z]=Pr⁡[xi=1∣zi=z](2)f(z)\equiv E[x_i\mid z_i=z]=\Pr[x_i=1\mid z_i=z] \tag{2}f(z)≡E[xi​∣zi​=z]=Pr[xi​=1∣zi​=z](2)

is known to be discontinuous at z0z_0z0​. The common feature of the two designs is stated as Assumption (RD): (i) the one-sided limits

x+≡lim⁡z→z0+E[xi∣zi=z],x−≡lim⁡z→z0−E[xi∣zi=z](3)x^+\equiv\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^+}E[x_i\mid z_i=z],\qquad x^-\equiv\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^-}E[x_i\mid z_i=z] \tag{3}x+≡z→z0+​lim​E[xi​∣zi​=z],x−≡z→z0−​lim​E[xi​∣zi​=z](3)

exist, and (ii) x+≠x−x^+\neq x^-x+=x−. The density of ziz_izi​ is assumed positive in a neighbourhood of z0z_0z0​ throughout. The corresponding limits of the outcome regression are:

y+≡lim⁡z→z0+E[yi∣zi=z],y−≡lim⁡z→z0−E[yi∣zi=z](4)y^+\equiv\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^+}E[y_i\mid z_i=z],\qquad y^-\equiv\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^-}E[y_i\mid z_i=z] \tag{4}y+≡z→z0+​lim​E[yi​∣zi​=z],y−≡z→z0−​lim​E[yi​∣zi​=z](4)

The analysis is carried out for the fuzzy design, and the sharp design is treated as the special case with x+=1x^+=1x+=1 and x−=0x^-=0x−=0.

Constant Treatment Effects

Suppose first that the treatment effect is the same for everyone, βi=β\beta_i=\betaβi​=β. Let e>0e>0e>0 be an arbitrarily small number. If persons close to the threshold are similar in the absence of treatment, the mean of αi\alpha_iαi​ just above z0z_0z0​ should be close to its mean just below. This motivates Assumption (A1): E[αi∣zi=z]E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z]E[αi​∣zi​=z] is continuous in zzz at z0z_0z0​.

Theorem 1. Suppose that βi\beta_iβi​ is fixed at β\betaβ and that Assumptions (RD) and (A1) hold. Then:

β=y+−y−x+−x−(5)\beta=\frac{y^+-y^-}{x^+-x^-} \tag{5}β=x+−x−y+−y−​(5)

The proof takes the mean difference in outcomes between persons just above and just below the discontinuity point:

E[yi∣zi=z0+e]−E[yi∣zi=z0−e]=β⋅{E[xi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi∣zi=z0−e]}+{E[αi∣zi=z0+e]−E[αi∣zi=z0−e]}(6)\begin{aligned} E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]&=\beta\cdot\left\{E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\}\\ &\quad+\left\{E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{6}E[yi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[yi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​=β⋅{E[xi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}+{E[αi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[αi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}​(6)

As eee goes to zero, the second bracket vanishes by (A1), so the jump in the outcome regression equals β\betaβ times the jump in the treatment probability, and the denominator is nonzero by (RD). The ratio of jumps is thus the treatment effect: any discontinuity of the outcome at z0z_0z0​ is attributed to the discontinuity in treatment, because everything else is assumed to move smoothly through the threshold. In the sharp design the result reduces to:

β=y+−y−(7)\beta=y^+-y^- \tag{7}β=y+−y−(7)

Variable Treatment Effects: Conditional Independence

When treatment effects are heterogeneous, the paper adds Assumption (A2): E[βi∣zi=z]E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z]E[βi​∣zi​=z], regarded as a function of zzz, is continuous at z0z_0z0​.

Theorem 2. Suppose that xix_ixi​ is independent of βi\beta_iβi​ conditional on ziz_izi​ near z0z_0z0​, and that Assumptions (RD), (A1) and (A2) hold. Then:

E[βi∣zi=z0]=y+−y−x+−x−(8)E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]=\frac{y^+-y^-}{x^+-x^-} \tag{8}E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]=x+−x−y+−y−​(8)

The proof repeats the previous decomposition with xi⋅βix_i\cdot\beta_ixi​⋅βi​ in place of β⋅xi\beta\cdot x_iβ⋅xi​. Conditional independence factorises the mean of the product on each side of the threshold:

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0±e]=E[βi∣zi=z0±e]⋅E[xi∣zi=z0±e](9)E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]=E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e] \tag{9}E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​±e]=E[βi​∣zi​=z0​±e]⋅E[xi​∣zi​=z0​±e](9)

The paper prints the conditioning event in this line as zi=z±ez_i=z\pm ezi​=z±e; the surrounding steps show that z0±ez_0\pm ez0​±e is meant. Letting eee go to zero, (A2) makes the first factor converge to E[βi∣zi=z0]E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]E[βi​∣zi​=z0​] from both sides, (A1) removes the difference in αi\alpha_iαi​, and the jump in the outcome regression equals E[βi∣zi=z0]E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]E[βi​∣zi​=z0​] times the jump in the treatment probability. The identified object is the average treatment effect at the threshold. In the sharp design:

E[βi∣zi=z0]=y+−y−(10)E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]=y^+-y^- \tag{10}E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]=y+−y−(10)

The conditional independence assumption says that individuals do not select into treatment on the basis of anticipated gains. The paper notes that this is routinely assumed in the matching literature but may be unrealistic when individuals self-select (it refers to Heckman, Lalonde and Smith 1999).

Variable Treatment Effects: Local Monotonicity and LATE

To allow selection on prospective gains, the paper follows Imbens and Angrist (1994). For each observation iii, treatment assignment is a deterministic function xi(z)x_i(z)xi​(z) of zzz, and the function differs across persons or groups of persons. Assumption (A3) has two parts: (i) (βi,xi(z))(\beta_i,x_i(z))(βi​,xi​(z)) is jointly independent of ziz_izi​ near z0z_0z0​; (ii) there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 such that:

xi(z0+e)≥xi(z0−e)for all 0<e<ε(11)x_i(z_0+e)\geq x_i(z_0-e)\qquad\text{for all }0<e<\varepsilon \tag{11}xi​(z0​+e)≥xi​(z0​−e)for all 0<e<ε(11)

Part (i) is a local version of instrument independence and part (ii) is local monotonicity: crossing the threshold from below never switches anyone out of treatment.

Theorem 3. Suppose that Assumptions (RD), (A1) and (A3) hold. Then:

lim⁡e→0+E[βi∣xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1]=y+−y−x+−x−(12)\lim_{e\rightarrow0^+}E[\beta_i\mid x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1]=\frac{y^+-y^-}{x^+-x^-} \tag{12}e→0+lim​E[βi​∣xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1]=x+−x−y+−y−​(12)

The proof invokes the reasoning in Imbens and Angrist (1994) to obtain:

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0−e]=E[βi∣xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1]⋅{E[xi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi∣zi=z0−e]}(13)\begin{aligned} E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]&=E[\beta_i\mid x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1]\\ &\quad\cdot\left\{E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{13}E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​=E[βi​∣xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1]⋅{E[xi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}​(13)

The intuition is as follows. By independence, conditioning on zi=z0±ez_i=z_0\pm ezi​=z0​±e only selects which potential treatment xi(z0±e)x_i(z_0\pm e)xi​(z0​±e) is realised, so the left-hand side is the mean of βi\beta_iβi​ times the change in potential treatment. By monotonicity that change is either zero or one, so the mean equals the average of βi\beta_iβi​ among those whose treatment changes, times the probability of a change, and that probability is the difference in treatment rates in the braces. Dividing by this difference and using (A1) to eliminate the difference in αi\alpha_iαi​ gives the theorem. For e>0e>0e>0 sufficiently small, the conditioning event {xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1}\{x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1\}{xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1} is the subgroup of persons for whom treatment changes discontinuously at z0z_0z0​. The ratio of jumps therefore identifies the local average treatment effect (LATE) at z0z_0z0​: the average effect for compliers at the threshold. Compared with Theorem 2, the independence of xix_ixi​ and βi\beta_iβi​ given ziz_izi​ is dropped, so selection on gains is allowed, at the cost of a parameter defined for a narrower subpopulation.

Discussion: Why Functional Form Restrictions Are Necessary

In every case identification comes from comparing persons arbitrarily close to z0z_0z0​ who did and did not receive treatment. Without further assumptions such as a common effect, treatment effects are identified only at z=z0z=z_0z=z0​, which the paper compares to identification at infinity (Chamberlain 1986). The paper then shows that the local continuity restriction on E[αi∣zi]E[\alpha_i\mid z_i]E[αi​∣zi​] together with the known discontinuity in E[xi∣zi]E[x_i\mid z_i]E[xi​∣zi​] is necessary. In a common effects model, write the outcome equation as:

yi=α(zi)+β⋅xi+vi(14)y_i=\alpha(z_i)+\beta\cdot x_i+v_i \tag{14}yi​=α(zi​)+β⋅xi​+vi​(14)

where α(zi)≡E[αi∣zi]\alpha(z_i)\equiv E[\alpha_i\mid z_i]α(zi​)≡E[αi​∣zi​] and vi≡αi−α(zi)v_i\equiv\alpha_i-\alpha(z_i)vi​≡αi​−α(zi​). The usual conditional mean independence restriction E[vi∣zi]=0E[v_i\mid z_i]=0E[vi​∣zi​]=0 does not identify β\betaβ. Consider another data generating process:

yi=α∗(zi)+0⋅xi+vi∗α∗(zi)≡α(zi)+β⋅E[xi∣zi],vi∗≡vi+β⋅{xi−E[xi∣zi]}(15)\begin{aligned} y_i&=\alpha^*(z_i)+0\cdot x_i+v_i^*\\ \alpha^*(z_i)&\equiv\alpha(z_i)+\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i],\qquad v_i^*\equiv v_i+\beta\cdot\left\{x_i-E[x_i\mid z_i]\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{15}yi​α∗(zi​)​=α∗(zi​)+0⋅xi​+vi∗​≡α(zi​)+β⋅E[xi​∣zi​],vi∗​≡vi​+β⋅{xi​−E[xi​∣zi​]}​(15)

The paper prints a minus sign in the definition of α∗(zi)\alpha^*(z_i)α∗(zi​); the plus sign is needed for the two models to coincide. The two models generate the same observables, and the error of the second also has zero conditional mean given ziz_izi​, but the treatment effect is β\betaβ in the first and 000 in the second. If E[vi∣zi]=0E[v_i\mid z_i]=0E[vi​∣zi​]=0 is the only restriction, the population cannot distinguish them. What rules out the second model is continuity: α∗(zi)\alpha^*(z_i)α∗(zi​) inherits the jump of E[xi∣zi]E[x_i\mid z_i]E[xi​∣zi​] at z0z_0z0​, so it violates (A1).

Estimation: Kernel Estimators and the Wald Estimator

For both designs the ratio (y+−y−)/(x+−x−)(y^+-y^-)/(x^+-x^-)(y+−y−)/(x+−x−) identifies the treatment effect at z=z0z=z_0z=z0​. Given consistent estimators y^+\hat{y}^+y^​+, y^−\hat{y}^-y^​−, x^+\hat{x}^+x^+ and x^−\hat{x}^-x^− of the four one-sided limits, the treatment effect is consistently estimated by:

β^=y^+−y^−x^+−x^−(16)\hat{\beta}=\frac{\hat{y}^+-\hat{y}^-}{\hat{x}^+-\hat{x}^-} \tag{16}β^​=x^+−x^−y^​+−y^​−​(16)

Any nonparametric estimator of the limits could be used. Consider first kernel regression (Nadaraya-Watson) estimators with one-sided uniform kernels. They are sample means on each side of the threshold:

y^+=∑i∈Syi⋅wi∑i∈Swi,y^−=∑i∈Syi⋅(1−wi)∑i∈S(1−wi)x^+=∑i∈Sxi⋅wi∑i∈Swi,x^−=∑i∈Sxi⋅(1−wi)∑i∈S(1−wi)(17)\begin{aligned} \hat{y}^+&=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}y_i\cdot w_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}w_i},\qquad\hat{y}^-=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}y_i\cdot(1-w_i)}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}(1-w_i)}\\ \hat{x}^+&=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_i\cdot w_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}w_i},\qquad\hat{x}^-=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}x_i\cdot(1-w_i)}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}(1-w_i)} \end{aligned} \tag{17}y^​+x^+​=∑i∈S​wi​∑i∈S​yi​⋅wi​​,y^​−=∑i∈S​(1−wi​)∑i∈S​yi​⋅(1−wi​)​=∑i∈S​wi​∑i∈S​xi​⋅wi​​,x^−=∑i∈S​(1−wi​)∑i∈S​xi​⋅(1−wi​)​​(17)

where S\mathcal{S}S is the subsample with z0−h<zi<z0+hz_0-h<z_i<z_0+hz0​−h<zi​<z0​+h, the indicator wi≡1(z0<zi<z0+h)w_i\equiv1(z_0<z_i<z_0+h)wi​≡1(z0​<zi​<z0​+h) marks observations above the threshold, and h>0h>0h>0 is the bandwidth. The resulting ratio is numerically equivalent to the instrumental variable estimator for the regression of yiy_iyi​ on a constant and xix_ixi​ that uses wiw_iwi​ as an instrument, applied to the subsample S\mathcal{S}S. This is the Wald estimator with a binary instrument, and the paper denotes it by β^w\hat{\beta}_wβ^​w​.

The RD design can justify this estimator even when the standard instrumental variable assumption is violated. Writing αi=E[αi]+vi=α+vi\alpha_i=E[\alpha_i]+v_i=\alpha+v_iαi​=E[αi​]+vi​=α+vi​, the common effect model is:

yi=α+xi⋅β+vi(18)y_i=\alpha+x_i\cdot\beta+v_i \tag{18}yi​=α+xi​⋅β+vi​(18)

Identification of β\betaβ does not require the error viv_ivi​ to be uncorrelated with ziz_izi​; all that is required is the continuity assumption (A1). As long as the researcher lets hhh shrink appropriately with the sample size, β^w\hat{\beta}_wβ^​w​ is consistent. It is motivated by a different principle from the usual Wald estimator, but for this particular kernel and subsample the two coincide numerically.

Inference differs, however. The estimator β^w\hat{\beta}_wβ^​w​ is asymptotically biased, like many estimators based on nonparametric regression, whereas the Wald estimator is asymptotically unbiased by assumption. The bias is aggravated by the boundary problem: under conventional assumptions on the kernel function, the bias of the standard kernel estimator is of order O(h)O(h)O(h) at boundary points and of order O(h2)O(h^2)O(h2) at interior points. In the RD problem every point of estimation is a boundary point, so the bias can be substantial in finite samples. The boundary bias formula implies that the bias is smallest when the one-sided derivatives of E[yi∣zi]E[y_i\mid z_i]E[yi​∣zi​] and E[xi∣zi]E[x_i\mid z_i]E[xi​∣zi​] around z0z_0z0​ are zero, so β^w\hat{\beta}_wβ^​w​ has a small bias only when αi\alpha_iαi​ is uncorrelated with ziz_izi​, that is, when ziz_izi​ is a proper instrument near the discontinuity. Conventional confidence intervals based on the asymptotic distribution of the Wald estimator would therefore have true coverage very different from nominal coverage. The paper notes that Porter (1998) proposes an alternative estimator for the sharp design with constant effects that has no boundary bias, under slightly stronger assumptions.

Estimation: Local Linear Regression

The paper proposes to estimate the limits by local linear regression (LLR), which Fan (1992) showed to have better boundary properties than kernel regression. The local linear estimator of y+y^+y+ is a^\hat{a}a^, where:

(a^,b^)≡argmin⁡a,b∑i=1n(yi−a−b(zi−z0))2K(zi−z0h)1(zi>z0)(19)(\hat{a},\hat{b})\equiv\operatorname*{argmin}_{a,b}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_i-a-b(z_i-z_0)\right)^2K\left(\frac{z_i-z_0}{h}\right)1(z_i>z_0) \tag{19}(a^,b^)≡a,bargmin​i=1∑n​(yi​−a−b(zi​−z0​))2K(hzi​−z0​​)1(zi​>z0​)(19)

Here K(⋅)K(\cdot)K(⋅) is a kernel function and h>0h>0h>0 is a bandwidth. The estimator fits a kernel-weighted line to the observations on one side of the threshold and takes its intercept at z0z_0z0​; the other three limits are estimated in the same way with xix_ixi​ in place of yiy_iyi​ and with the indicator 1(zi<z0)1(z_i<z_0)1(zi​<z0​). Because the slope absorbs the first-order term, the bias is of smaller order than that of the kernel estimator, so LLR is more rate-efficient. A further advantage is that the bias does not depend on the design density of the data.

For the distribution theory, define the regression functions:

m(z)≡E[yi∣zi=z],p(z)≡E[xi∣zi=z](20)m(z)\equiv E[y_i\mid z_i=z],\qquad p(z)\equiv E[x_i\mid z_i=z] \tag{20}m(z)≡E[yi​∣zi​=z],p(z)≡E[xi​∣zi​=z](20)

The paper prints the second definition as p(z)≡[xi∣zi=z]p(z)\equiv[x_i\mid z_i=z]p(z)≡[xi​∣zi​=z], omitting the expectation operator. Their one-sided limits at z0z_0z0​ are written m+(z0)m^+(z_0)m+(z0​), m−(z0)m^-(z_0)m−(z0​), p+(z0)p^+(z_0)p+(z0​) and p−(z0)p^-(z_0)p−(z0​), which are the same objects as y+y^+y+, y−y^-y−, x+x^+x+ and x−x^-x−. The one-sided limits of the conditional variance and covariance are:

σ2+(z0)=lim⁡z→z0+var⁡[yi∣zi=z],σ2−(z0)=lim⁡z→z0−var⁡[yi∣zi=z]η+(z0)=lim⁡z→z0+cov⁡[yi,xi∣zi=z],η−(z0)=lim⁡z→z0−cov⁡[yi,xi∣zi=z](21)\begin{aligned} \sigma^{2+}(z_0)&=\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^+}\operatorname{var}[y_i\mid z_i=z],\qquad\sigma^{2-}(z_0)=\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^-}\operatorname{var}[y_i\mid z_i=z]\\ \eta^+(z_0)&=\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^+}\operatorname{cov}[y_i,x_i\mid z_i=z],\qquad\eta^-(z_0)=\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^-}\operatorname{cov}[y_i,x_i\mid z_i=z] \end{aligned} \tag{21}σ2+(z0​)η+(z0​)​=z→z0+​lim​var[yi​∣zi​=z],σ2−(z0​)=z→z0−​lim​var[yi​∣zi​=z]=z→z0+​lim​cov[yi​,xi​∣zi​=z],η−(z0​)=z→z0−​lim​cov[yi​,xi​∣zi​=z]​(21)

Theorem 4 (Asymptotic Distribution). The assumptions are the following. (i) For z>z0z>z_0z>z0​, m(z)m(z)m(z) and p(z)p(z)p(z) are twice continuously differentiable, and there exists M>0M>0M>0 such that these functions and their first and second derivatives are uniformly bounded on (z0,z0+M](z_0,z_0+M](z0​,z0​+M]; the same holds on [z0−M,z0)[z_0-M,z_0)[z0​−M,z0​). (iii) The density f(z)f(z)f(z) of ziz_izi​ is continuous and bounded near z0z_0z0​, and bounded away from zero near z0z_0z0​. (iv) K(⋅)K(\cdot)K(⋅) is continuous, symmetric and nonnegative-valued with compact support. (v) The conditional variance σ2(zi)=var⁡(yi∣zi)\sigma^2(z_i)=\operatorname{var}(y_i\mid z_i)σ2(zi​)=var(yi​∣zi​) and the conditional covariance η(zi)=cov⁡(yi,xi∣zi)\eta(z_i)=\operatorname{cov}(y_i,x_i\mid z_i)η(zi​)=cov(yi​,xi​∣zi​) are uniformly bounded near z0z_0z0​, and their one-sided limits at z0z_0z0​ exist and are finite. The structure of the result is that of a delta-method expansion of the ratio. The numerator y^+−y^−\hat{y}^+-\hat{y}^-y^​+−y^​− enters with weight 1/(x+−x−)1/(x^+-x^-)1/(x+−x−) and the denominator x^+−x^−\hat{x}^+-\hat{x}^-x^+−x^− with weight −(y+−y−)/(x+−x−)2-(y^+-y^-)/(x^+-x^-)^2−(y+−y−)/(x+−x−)2, which explains the two terms of μf\mu_fμf​ and the three terms of Ωf\Omega_fΩf​ (variance of the outcome part, covariance, and variance of the treatment part, where the conditional variance of the binary xix_ixi​ is p(1−p)p(1-p)p(1−p)). Each one-sided LLR estimator has a bias proportional to h2h^2h2 times the one-sided second derivative, so with hhh of order n−1/5n^{-1/5}n−1/5 the bias and the standard deviation are both of order n−2/5n^{-2/5}n−2/5, and the limit distribution has mean μf\mu_fμf​ instead of zero. The variance is inversely proportional to the density f(z0)f(z_0)f(z0​) and to ϱ\varrhoϱ, and it grows without bound as x+−x−x^+-x^-x+−x− goes to zero, the RD analogue of a weak instrument. The two sides of the threshold contribute additively because they use disjoint sets of observations. The proof is not given in the paper; it is available in Hahn, Todd and Van der Klaauw (1999) or from the authors.

Summary and Scope

The RD method identifies mean treatment impacts for a subgroup of the population under minimal assumptions, and it bypasses questions of model specification, both which variables to include in the outcome model and in what functional form. Its limitation is that it identifies the treatment effect only locally, at the point where the probability of treatment changes discontinuously. In some cases this local parameter is exactly the one of interest, for example when the policy under consideration is a small change in programme rules such as lowering or raising the entry threshold, so that one wants the effect for the subpopulation affected by the change.

Each person has two potential outcomes, y1iy_{1i}y1i​ with treatment and y0iy_{0i}y0i​ without, and the indicator xix_ixi​ selects which of them is observed. The starting point is this switching rule:

yi=xi⋅y1i+(1−xi)⋅y0iy_i=x_i\cdot y_{1i}+(1-x_i)\cdot y_{0i}yi​=xi​⋅y1i​+(1−xi​)⋅y0i​

Collect the part that does not depend on xix_ixi​ and the part that multiplies it, then rename:

yi=y0i+xi⋅(y1i−y0i)=αi+xi⋅βi\begin{aligned} y_i&=y_{0i}+x_i\cdot(y_{1i}-y_{0i})\\ &=\alpha_i+x_i\cdot\beta_i \end{aligned}yi​​=y0i​+xi​⋅(y1i​−y0i​)=αi​+xi​⋅βi​​

with αi≡y0i\alpha_i\equiv y_{0i}αi​≡y0i​ and βi≡y1i−y0i\beta_i\equiv y_{1i}-y_{0i}βi​≡y1i​−y0i​. The result is a random-coefficient regression: the intercept αi\alpha_iαi​ and the slope βi\beta_iβi​ both vary across persons, and neither is observed because only one of the two potential outcomes is ever seen. No assumption has been made so far. All the content comes later, from restrictions on how αi\alpha_iαi​ and βi\beta_iβi​ vary with ziz_izi​ near z0z_0z0​ (Assumptions (A1), (A2) and (A3)). Setting βi=β\beta_i=\betaβi​=β gives the common-effect model used in equations (5), (14) and (18).

This equation defines the treatment regression in the fuzzy design. Because xix_ixi​ only takes the values zero and one, its conditional mean is a conditional probability:

E[xi∣zi=z]=1⋅Pr⁡[xi=1∣zi=z]+0⋅Pr⁡[xi=0∣zi=z]E[x_i\mid z_i=z]=1\cdot\Pr[x_i=1\mid z_i=z]+0\cdot\Pr[x_i=0\mid z_i=z]E[xi​∣zi​=z]=1⋅Pr[xi​=1∣zi​=z]+0⋅Pr[xi​=0∣zi​=z]

so f(z)f(z)f(z) lies between zero and one and is the share of persons with assignment variable zzz who are treated (the propensity score as a function of zzz). The symbol fff is the same one used for the deterministic rule xi=f(zi)x_i=f(z_i)xi​=f(zi​) of the sharp design, which is the special case in which f(z)f(z)f(z) only takes the values zero and one. In the fuzzy design f(z)f(z)f(z) is strictly between zero and one on at least one side of z0z_0z0​, because variables that the econometrician does not see also affect assignment. What matters for identification is not the level of fff but its jump at z0z_0z0​, which equation (3) formalises through the one-sided limits x+x^+x+ and x−x^-x−. A simple example: a scholarship is offered with probability 0.20.20.2 below a test-score cutoff and 0.70.70.7 above it, so that x+−x−=0.5x^+-x^-=0.5x+−x−=0.5. Note that in Theorem 4 the note (following the paper) reuses the letter fff for the density of ziz_izi​, as in equation (27); the two objects are unrelated.

These are the right and left limits at the threshold of the treatment probability f(z)f(z)f(z) of equation (2). The limit x+x^+x+ is the treatment rate among persons whose ziz_izi​ is just above z0z_0z0​, and x−x^-x− is the rate among persons just below. Assumption (RD) has two parts: (i) both limits exist, and (ii) they differ, x+≠x−x^+\neq x^-x+=x−. Part (ii) is the defining feature of the design and plays the role of instrument relevance in instrumental variable estimation: the difference

x+−x−x^+-x^-x+−x−

is the denominator of the identification results in equations (5), (8) and (12), so it has to be nonzero. The value of fff at z0z_0z0​ itself is irrelevant; only the two one-sided limits enter. The maintained assumption that the density of ziz_izi​ is positive around z0z_0z0​ guarantees that there are observations on both sides arbitrarily close to the threshold, so that conditional means given zi=zz_i=zzi​=z are well defined there. In the sharp design x+=1x^+=1x+=1 and x−=0x^-=0x−=0 (or the reverse), so the jump has absolute size one; in the fuzzy design the jump is smaller than one in absolute value. The sign is not restricted by (RD); under the monotonicity condition in equation (11) one has x+>x−x^+>x^-x+>x−. The estimators in equations (17) and (19) are sample analogues of these limits.

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0±e]=E[βi∣zi=z0±e]⋅E[xi∣zi=z0±e]E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]=E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​±e]=E[βi​∣zi​=z0​±e]⋅E[xi​∣zi​=z0​±e]

By (A2) the factor E[βi∣zi=z0±e]E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]E[βi​∣zi​=z0​±e] converges to E[βi∣zi=z0]E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]E[βi​∣zi​=z0​] from both sides; by (RD) the factor E[xi∣zi=z0±e]E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]E[xi​∣zi​=z0​±e] converges to x+x^+x+ and x−x^-x− respectively; by (A1) the bracket in αi\alpha_iαi​ converges to zero. Hence

y+−y−=E[βi∣zi=z0]⋅x+−E[βi∣zi=z0]⋅x−=E[βi∣zi=z0]⋅(x+−x−)\begin{aligned} y^+-y^-&=E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]\cdot x^+-E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]\cdot x^-\\ &=E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]\cdot(x^+-x^-) \end{aligned}y+−y−​=E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]⋅x+−E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]⋅x−=E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]⋅(x+−x−)​

Dividing by x+−x−≠0x^+-x^-\neq0x+−x−=0 gives

E[βi∣zi=z0]=y+−y−x+−x−E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]=\frac{y^+-y^-}{x^+-x^-}E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]=x+−x−y+−y−​

Assumption (A2) is what allows the common factor to be taken out: without it the mean effect just above and just below the threshold could differ and the two products would not combine.

The claim is that the conditional mean of a product factorises. Fix a value zzz near z0z_0z0​. Conditional independence of xix_ixi​ and βi\beta_iβi​ given zi=zz_i=zzi​=z means that the conditional joint distribution is the product of the conditional marginals, so for the product of the two variables

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z]=E[xi∣zi=z]⋅E[βi∣zi=z]E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z]=E[x_i\mid z_i=z]\cdot E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z]E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z]=E[xi​∣zi​=z]⋅E[βi​∣zi​=z]

A direct way to see it uses the fact that xix_ixi​ is binary. By the law of iterated expectations,

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z]=Pr⁡[xi=1∣zi=z]⋅E[βi∣xi=1,zi=z]=E[xi∣zi=z]⋅E[βi∣zi=z]\begin{aligned} E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z]&=\Pr[x_i=1\mid z_i=z]\cdot E[\beta_i\mid x_i=1,z_i=z]\\ &=E[x_i\mid z_i=z]\cdot E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z] \end{aligned}E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z]​=Pr[xi​=1∣zi​=z]⋅E[βi​∣xi​=1,zi​=z]=E[xi​∣zi​=z]⋅E[βi​∣zi​=z]​

where the second line uses E[βi∣xi=1,zi=z]=E[βi∣zi=z]E[\beta_i\mid x_i=1,z_i=z]=E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z]E[βi​∣xi​=1,zi​=z]=E[βi​∣zi​=z], that is, the treated at a given zzz have the same mean gain as everyone at that zzz. Only this mean-independence is actually needed. Evaluating at z=z0+ez=z_0+ez=z0​+e and z=z0−ez=z_0-ez=z0​−e gives

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0±e]=E[βi∣zi=z0±e]⋅E[xi∣zi=z0±e]E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]=E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0\pm e]E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​±e]=E[βi​∣zi​=z0​±e]⋅E[xi​∣zi​=z0​±e]

The conditioning point must be z0±ez_0\pm ez0​±e for the line to be usable in the proof of equation (8), whose preceding step is evaluated at z0±ez_0\pm ez0​±e. The published paper prints z±ez\pm ez±e here; the note's correction to z0±ez_0\pm ez0​±e is right.

In the sharp design everyone just above z0z_0z0​ is treated and no one just below, so the limits in equation (3) are

x+=1,x−=0x^+=1,\qquad x^-=0x+=1,x−=0

Substituting into equation (8):

E[βi∣zi=z0]=y+−y−1−0=y+−y−E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0]=\frac{y^+-y^-}{1-0}=y^+-y^-E[βi​∣zi​=z0​]=1−0y+−y−​=y+−y−

In the sharp design the independence condition of Theorem 2 holds trivially, because given ziz_izi​ the treatment xix_ixi​ is a constant and a constant is independent of anything. The result can therefore be obtained from (A1) and (A2) alone: just above the threshold E[yi∣zi=z]=E[αi∣zi=z]+E[βi∣zi=z]E[y_i\mid z_i=z]=E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z]+E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z]E[yi​∣zi​=z]=E[αi​∣zi​=z]+E[βi​∣zi​=z], just below it E[yi∣zi=z]=E[αi∣zi=z]E[y_i\mid z_i=z]=E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z]E[yi​∣zi​=z]=E[αi​∣zi​=z], and continuity of both conditional means at z0z_0z0​ gives the display. This is the average treatment effect for persons at the threshold.

This is the monotonicity part (ii) of Assumption (A3). The object xi(z)x_i(z)xi​(z) is the potential treatment status of person iii if the assignment variable were set to zzz: a deterministic zero-one function of zzz that differs across persons, in the way potential treatments are indexed by the instrument in Imbens and Angrist (1994). The observed treatment is xi=xi(zi)x_i=x_i(z_i)xi​=xi​(zi​). The condition says that for every pair of points placed symmetrically around the threshold within distance ε\varepsilonε, moving from z0−ez_0-ez0​−e to z0+ez_0+ez0​+e either leaves a person's treatment unchanged or switches it on, and never switches it off. Hence the change

xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)∈{0,1}x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)\in\{0,1\}xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)∈{0,1}

and the value −1-1−1 (a defier) is ruled out. Persons with a change of one are the compliers at the threshold; persons with a change of zero are always-takers or never-takers locally. The condition is local, since it is required only for 0<e<ε0<e<\varepsilon0<e<ε, and it is a restriction on behaviour and not on functional form. It is what turns the mean of βi\beta_iβi​ times the change in potential treatment into a complier average in equation (13). Without it, gains of compliers and defiers would enter with opposite signs and the ratio in equation (12) would not be an average of treatment effects. Together with (RD) it implies x+>x−x^+>x^-x+>x−.

Take conditional means in equation (1) at z0+ez_0+ez0​+e and z0−ez_0-ez0​−e and subtract, as in the proof of equation (8):

E[yi∣zi=z0+e]−E[yi∣zi=z0−e]={E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0−e]}+{E[αi∣zi=z0+e]−E[αi∣zi=z0−e]}\begin{aligned} E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]&=\left\{E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\}\\ &\quad+\left\{E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\} \end{aligned}E[yi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[yi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​={E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}+{E[αi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[αi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}​

Replace the first bracket by equation (13), which holds under (A3) for 0<e<ε0<e<\varepsilon0<e<ε:

E[yi∣zi=z0+e]−E[yi∣zi=z0−e]=E[βi∣xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1]⋅{E[xi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi∣zi=z0−e]}+{E[αi∣zi=z0+e]−E[αi∣zi=z0−e]}\begin{aligned} E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]&=E[\beta_i\mid x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1]\cdot\left\{E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\}\\ &\quad+\left\{E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\} \end{aligned}E[yi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[yi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​=E[βi​∣xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1]⋅{E[xi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}+{E[αi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[αi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}​

By (RD) the difference in treatment rates converges to x+−x−≠0x^+-x^-\neq0x+−x−=0, so it is nonzero for all small eee and one can divide by it:

E[βi∣xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1]=E[yi∣zi=z0+e]−E[yi∣zi=z0−e]−{E[αi∣zi=z0+e]−E[αi∣zi=z0−e]}E[xi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi∣zi=z0−e]E[\beta_i\mid x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1]=\frac{E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[y_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]-\left\{E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[\alpha_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\}}{E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]}E[βi​∣xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1]=E[xi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​∣zi​=z0​−e]E[yi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[yi​∣zi​=z0​−e]−{E[αi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[αi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}​

Let eee go to zero from above. The bracket in αi\alpha_iαi​ vanishes by (A1), the outcome difference converges to y+−y−y^+-y^-y+−y− and the denominator to x+−x−x^+-x^-x+−x−. The right-hand side has a limit, so the left-hand side has one as well:

lim⁡e→0+E[βi∣xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1]=y+−y−x+−x−\lim_{e\rightarrow0^+}E[\beta_i\mid x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1]=\frac{y^+-y^-}{x^+-x^-}e→0+lim​E[βi​∣xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1]=x+−x−y+−y−​

Two remarks on what is assumed. First, the conditioning event has positive probability for small eee because that probability equals the difference in treatment rates, which tends to x+−x−>0x^+-x^->0x+−x−>0. Second, (A2) is not listed among the assumptions, but it is not really dispensed with: part (i) of (A3) makes the distribution of βi\beta_iβi​ the same at every zzz near z0z_0z0​, so E[βi∣zi=z]E[\beta_i\mid z_i=z]E[βi​∣zi​=z] is constant there and (A2) holds automatically. What Theorem 3 drops relative to Theorem 2 is the independence between xix_ixi​ and βi\beta_iβi​ given ziz_izi​.

The paper only cites Imbens and Angrist (1994); the steps are as follows. Write Δi(e)≡xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)\Delta_i(e)\equiv x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)Δi​(e)≡xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e) for the change in potential treatment. The observed treatment is xi=xi(zi)x_i=x_i(z_i)xi​=xi​(zi​), so on the event zi=z0+ez_i=z_0+ezi​=z0​+e it equals xi(z0+e)x_i(z_0+e)xi​(z0​+e). By part (i) of (A3) the pair (βi,xi(⋅))(\beta_i,x_i(\cdot))(βi​,xi​(⋅)) has the same distribution at every value of ziz_izi​ near z0z_0z0​, so conditioning on ziz_izi​ can be dropped (all unconditional means below are means over persons with ziz_izi​ in this neighbourhood):

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0+e]=E[xi(z0+e)⋅βi∣zi=z0+e]=E[xi(z0+e)⋅βi]E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0−e]=E[xi(z0−e)⋅βi∣zi=z0−e]=E[xi(z0−e)⋅βi]\begin{aligned} E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]&=E[x_i(z_0+e)\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]=E[x_i(z_0+e)\cdot\beta_i]\\ E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]&=E[x_i(z_0-e)\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]=E[x_i(z_0-e)\cdot\beta_i] \end{aligned}E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​+e]E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​=E[xi​(z0​+e)⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​+e]=E[xi​(z0​+e)⋅βi​]=E[xi​(z0​−e)⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​−e]=E[xi​(z0​−e)⋅βi​]​

Subtract the second line from the first:

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0−e]=E[βi⋅Δi(e)]E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]=E[\beta_i\cdot\Delta_i(e)]E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​−e]=E[βi​⋅Δi​(e)]

By monotonicity, equation (11), Δi(e)\Delta_i(e)Δi​(e) is either zero or one for 0<e<ε0<e<\varepsilon0<e<ε, so the mean of the product is the mean of βi\beta_iβi​ on the event Δi(e)=1\Delta_i(e)=1Δi​(e)=1 times the probability of that event:

E[βi⋅Δi(e)]=E[βi∣Δi(e)=1]⋅Pr⁡[Δi(e)=1]E[\beta_i\cdot\Delta_i(e)]=E[\beta_i\mid\Delta_i(e)=1]\cdot\Pr[\Delta_i(e)=1]E[βi​⋅Δi​(e)]=E[βi​∣Δi​(e)=1]⋅Pr[Δi​(e)=1]

For the same reason the probability equals the mean of Δi(e)\Delta_i(e)Δi​(e), and by independence again this is the difference in observed treatment rates:

Pr⁡[Δi(e)=1]=E[xi(z0+e)]−E[xi(z0−e)]=E[xi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi∣zi=z0−e]\begin{aligned} \Pr[\Delta_i(e)=1]&=E[x_i(z_0+e)]-E[x_i(z_0-e)]\\ &=E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0-e] \end{aligned}Pr[Δi​(e)=1]​=E[xi​(z0​+e)]−E[xi​(z0​−e)]=E[xi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​

Combining the last three displays:

E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi⋅βi∣zi=z0−e]=E[βi∣xi(z0+e)−xi(z0−e)=1]⋅{E[xi∣zi=z0+e]−E[xi∣zi=z0−e]}\begin{aligned} E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\cdot\beta_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]&=E[\beta_i\mid x_i(z_0+e)-x_i(z_0-e)=1]\\ &\quad\cdot\left\{E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0+e]-E[x_i\mid z_i=z_0-e]\right\} \end{aligned}E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​⋅βi​∣zi​=z0​−e]​=E[βi​∣xi​(z0​+e)−xi​(z0​−e)=1]⋅{E[xi​∣zi​=z0​+e]−E[xi​∣zi​=z0​−e]}​

The note's verbal argument is this derivation and is correct. If defiers were allowed, Δi(e)\Delta_i(e)Δi​(e) could equal −1-1−1 and the left-hand side would be a difference between complier and defier gains, weighted by their shares, with no interpretation as an average effect.

Start from equation (1) with a common effect, yi=αi+β⋅xiy_i=\alpha_i+\beta\cdot x_iyi​=αi​+β⋅xi​. Split the person-specific intercept into its conditional mean given ziz_izi​ and a deviation:

αi=α(zi)+vi,α(zi)≡E[αi∣zi],vi≡αi−α(zi)\alpha_i=\alpha(z_i)+v_i,\qquad\alpha(z_i)\equiv E[\alpha_i\mid z_i],\qquad v_i\equiv\alpha_i-\alpha(z_i)αi​=α(zi​)+vi​,α(zi​)≡E[αi​∣zi​],vi​≡αi​−α(zi​)

Substituting gives a partially linear regression:

yi=α(zi)+β⋅xi+viy_i=\alpha(z_i)+\beta\cdot x_i+v_iyi​=α(zi​)+β⋅xi​+vi​

The error has zero conditional mean by construction, not by assumption:

E[vi∣zi]=E[αi∣zi]−α(zi)=0E[v_i\mid z_i]=E[\alpha_i\mid z_i]-\alpha(z_i)=0E[vi​∣zi​]=E[αi​∣zi​]−α(zi​)=0

So the restriction E[vi∣zi]=0E[v_i\mid z_i]=0E[vi​∣zi​]=0 carries no information. It also says nothing about E[vi∣xi,zi]E[v_i\mid x_i,z_i]E[vi​∣xi​,zi​]: the error may be correlated with xix_ixi​ given ziz_izi​, which is the selection problem. The unknown function α(zi)\alpha(z_i)α(zi​) is where (A1) bites, since (A1) says that α(⋅)\alpha(\cdot)α(⋅) is continuous at z0z_0z0​. Equation (15) shows that without such a restriction on α(⋅)\alpha(\cdot)α(⋅) the parameter β\betaβ is not identified.

The aim is to rewrite the same observable yiy_iyi​ as a model with zero treatment effect. Start from equation (14) and add and subtract β⋅E[xi∣zi]\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i]β⋅E[xi​∣zi​]:

yi=α(zi)+β⋅xi+vi={α(zi)+β⋅E[xi∣zi]}+0⋅xi+{vi+β⋅(xi−E[xi∣zi])}\begin{aligned} y_i&=\alpha(z_i)+\beta\cdot x_i+v_i\\ &=\left\{\alpha(z_i)+\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i]\right\}+0\cdot x_i+\left\{v_i+\beta\cdot\left(x_i-E[x_i\mid z_i]\right)\right\} \end{aligned}yi​​=α(zi​)+β⋅xi​+vi​={α(zi​)+β⋅E[xi​∣zi​]}+0⋅xi​+{vi​+β⋅(xi​−E[xi​∣zi​])}​

The second brace is the vi∗v_i^*vi∗​ of the note. The first brace is the intercept function that makes the two models coincide, and it has a plus sign:

α∗(zi)=α(zi)+β⋅E[xi∣zi]\alpha^*(z_i)=\alpha(z_i)+\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i]α∗(zi​)=α(zi​)+β⋅E[xi​∣zi​]

The published paper prints α∗(zi)≡α(zi)−β⋅E[xi∣zi]\alpha^*(z_i)\equiv\alpha(z_i)-\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i]α∗(zi​)≡α(zi​)−β⋅E[xi​∣zi​]. With that minus sign the two data generating processes are not the same, because

{α(zi)−β⋅E[xi∣zi]}+vi+β⋅(xi−E[xi∣zi])=yi−2β⋅E[xi∣zi]\left\{\alpha(z_i)-\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i]\right\}+v_i+\beta\cdot\left(x_i-E[x_i\mid z_i]\right)=y_i-2\beta\cdot E[x_i\mid z_i]{α(zi​)−β⋅E[xi​∣zi​]}+vi​+β⋅(xi​−E[xi​∣zi​])=yi​−2β⋅E[xi​∣zi​]

which differs from yiy_iyi​ whenever β≠0\beta\neq0β=0. The minus sign is a misprint in the paper, which the note corrects; the argument requires the plus sign. With the plus sign the rest goes through. The new error has zero conditional mean:

E[vi∗∣zi]=E[vi∣zi]+β⋅(E[xi∣zi]−E[xi∣zi])=0E[v_i^*\mid z_i]=E[v_i\mid z_i]+\beta\cdot\left(E[x_i\mid z_i]-E[x_i\mid z_i]\right)=0E[vi∗​∣zi​]=E[vi​∣zi​]+β⋅(E[xi​∣zi​]−E[xi​∣zi​])=0

So both models satisfy the mean-independence restriction and generate the same distribution of (yi,xi,zi)(y_i,x_i,z_i)(yi​,xi​,zi​), but the coefficient on xix_ixi​ is β\betaβ in one and 000 in the other. What separates them is continuity. The jump of the new intercept function at the threshold is

lim⁡z→z0+α∗(z)−lim⁡z→z0−α∗(z)=β⋅(x+−x−)≠0\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^+}\alpha^*(z)-\lim_{z\rightarrow z_0^-}\alpha^*(z)=\beta\cdot(x^+-x^-)\neq0z→z0+​lim​α∗(z)−z→z0−​lim​α∗(z)=β⋅(x+−x−)=0

when α(⋅)\alpha(\cdot)α(⋅) is continuous and β≠0\beta\neq0β=0, so α∗(⋅)\alpha^*(\cdot)α∗(⋅) violates (A1). (With either sign α∗\alpha^*α∗ is discontinuous, so the misprint does not affect this last step.)

This is the plug-in (analogue) estimator of the ratio of jumps that equations (5), (8) and (12) show to be the treatment effect at z=z0z=z_0z=z0​. Each of the four one-sided limits defined in equations (3) and (4) is replaced by a nonparametric estimate: y^+\hat{y}^+y^​+ and x^+\hat{x}^+x^+ use only observations with ziz_izi​ just above z0z_0z0​, and y^−\hat{y}^-y^​− and x^−\hat{x}^-x^− only those just below. Consistency follows from the continuous mapping theorem: the map

(a1,a2,b1,b2)↦a1−a2b1−b2(a_1,a_2,b_1,b_2)\mapsto\frac{a_1-a_2}{b_1-b_2}(a1​,a2​,b1​,b2​)↦b1​−b2​a1​−a2​​

is continuous wherever b1≠b2b_1\neq b_2b1​=b2​, and x+≠x−x^+\neq x^-x+=x− by (RD), so if the four estimators converge in probability to the four limits then β^\hat{\beta}β^​ converges in probability to (y+−y−)/(x+−x−)(y^+-y^-)/(x^+-x^-)(y+−y−)/(x+−x−). The estimator has the form of a Wald or indirect least squares estimator: a reduced-form jump in the outcome divided by a first-stage jump in treatment. In the sharp design the denominator is known to equal one and need not be estimated. Since the estimand is the same ratio in all three theorems, the estimator does not depend on which set of identifying assumptions one adopts; only its interpretation (common effect, average effect at the threshold, or LATE) changes. The choice of the nonparametric method matters for bias and inference: equation (17) uses one-sided kernel means, equation (19) local linear regression, and equation (23) gives the limiting distribution in the latter case.

This fixes the rate at which the bandwidth shrinks with the sample size, and introduces the constant ϱ\varrhoϱ (which must be positive), not to be confused with the bias constants ρ+\rho^+ρ+ and ρ−\rho^-ρ− of equation (26). The exponent comes from balancing bias against sampling noise. A one-sided local linear estimator has bias of order h2h^2h2 and, because it uses about nhnhnh observations, variance of order 1/(nh)1/(nh)1/(nh). Its mean squared error is therefore of order

A bandwidth shrinking faster than n−1/5n^{-1/5}n−1/5 (undersmoothing) would remove the bias from the limit at the cost of a slower rate. The rate n2/5n^{2/5}n2/5 is slower than the parametric rate n1/2n^{1/2}n1/2 because only observations near z0z_0z0​ are informative.

with means and variances given in the derivations of equations (24) and (25).
